# metafor

```{r}
library(metafor)
library(dmetar)
data("SleepProblems")
```

## Confirmatory Factor Analysis

### Stage 1

1.  pool correlation matrices using `tssem1`

```{r}
cfa1 <- tssem1(SleepProblems$data, 
               SleepProblems$n, 
               method="REM",
               RE.type = "Diag")

summary(cfa1)
```

```{r}
# Extract the fixed coefficients (correlations)
fixed.coefs <- coef(cfa1, "fixed")

# Make a symmetric matrix
fc.mat <- vec2symMat(fixed.coefs, diag = FALSE)

# Label rows and columns
dimnames(fc.mat)[[1]] <- c("Quality", "Latency", 
                           "Efficiency", "DTDysf", "HypSomnia")
dimnames(fc.mat)[[2]] <- c("Quality", "Latency", 
                           "Efficiency", "DTDysf", "HypSomnia")

# Print correlation matrix (3 digits)
round(fc.mat, 3)
```

We can now see the pooled correlation matrix for our variables. Looking back at the model output, we also see that all correlation coefficients are significant (p\< 0.05), except one: the correlation between sleep quality and daytime dysfunction was not significant. From the perspective of our assumed model, this makes sense, because we expect these variables to load on different factors. We also see that the I2 values of the different estimates are very large (65-93%).

### Stage 2

After pooling the correlation matrices, we have to specify our model.

We have to use RAM formulation and specify the A, S and F matrices.

To fill the fields in each of these matrices, it's best to construct an empty matrix first.

Structure-wise, all matrices we define do not only contain the observed variables, but also the assumed latent variables.

```{r}
# Create vector of column/row names
dims <- c("Quality", "Latency", "Efficiency", 
          "DTDysf", "HypSomnia", "f_Insomnia", "f_Lassitude")

# Create 7x7 matrix of zeros
mat <- matrix(rep(0, 7*7), nrow = 7, ncol = 7)

# Label the rows and columns
dimnames(mat)[[1]] <- dimnames(mat)[[2]] <- dims
mat
```
